query: For a titanium- and nickel-containing high-entropy alloy in a single-phase solid-solution state, whose elevated-temperature mechanical performance remains unestablished when titanium and nickel serve as primary constituents rather than additions, what single testable intervention hypothesis could produce better mechanical properties under elevated-temperature or extreme-environment testing than the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, mechanism, predicted relative outcome, applicable composition and test-regime boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, conformal oxidation‐resistant coating on the titanium–nickel single‐phase high-entropy alloy will suppress high-temperature surface oxidation and impurity ingress, thereby preserving the microstructure and enhancing the elevated‐temperature mechanical properties relative to the uncoated alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase Ti–Ni high-entropy alloy prepared by conventional means (e.g., arc melting or powder metallurgy) with titanium and nickel as the primary constituents.
generation.intervention: Deposit a ~100 nm thick, uniform alumina (Al₂O₃) coating via atomic layer deposition (ALD) on the alloy’s surface.
generation.conditions: Expose both coated and uncoated samples to elevated-temperature testing (e.g., tensile or compressive tests conducted at 600–1000°C in an air or slightly oxidizing atmosphere) after subjecting them to a thermal exposure (e.g., holding at 800°C for 50 hours) to simulate extreme-environment service.
generation.structural_mediator: The alumina layer serves as a barrier that prevents oxygen and other impurities from penetrating into the alloy’s surface and grain boundaries, thereby reducing oxidation-driven phase segregation or PFZ (precipitate free zone) formation at the boundaries.
generation.mechanism: By reducing interstitial oxygen and nitrogen ingress during high-temperature exposure, the protective alumina coating limits detrimental oxidative reactions at the surface and along grain boundaries. This preservation of the pristine single-phase microstructure mitigates weakening mechanisms (such as impurity-induced softening) and maintains dislocation mobility conducive to high yield strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coated alloy is expected to exhibit a higher yield strength and improved ductility at elevated temperatures compared to the uncoated baseline, as it will show less surface oxidation and minimized grain-boundary degradation.
generation.baseline: The as-processed Ti–Ni high-entropy alloy without any protective coating, which under high-temperature or extreme-environment conditions is prone to oxidation and impurity pickup that degrade its mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: Applicable to single-phase Ti–Ni HEAs where titanium and nickel are primary constituents; the intervention is tested under high-temperature conditions (600–1000°C) and in atmospheres where oxidation is a concern. It does not address other potential failure modes such as creep at very long durations or mechanical fatigue under cyclic loading.
generation.uncertainty: While the expected beneficial effect is supported by general principles of oxidation barrier coatings and analogous observations in other high-temperature HEAs, the quantitative magnitude of improvement and the long-term adherence/stability of the ALD alumina under cyclic thermal loading are not yet established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Ti–Ni high-entropy alloy samples: one set receives an approximately 100-nm thick alumina coating via ALD, while the other set remains uncoated. Subject both sets to a thermal aging treatment at 800°C for 50 hours in an air or mildly oxidizing atmosphere, followed by elevated-temperature mechanical testing (e.g., tensile or compressive tests at 800°C). Compare the mechanical properties and microstructural integrity of the two sets using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM).
measurements: Yield strength and ductility (%) during elevated-temperature tests
Extent and nature of oxidation (oxide scale thickness, grain boundary degradation) via SEM/TEM
Microstructural analysis to observe any phase changes or impurity-induced degradation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in elevated-temperature yield strength and ductility—and if microscopy shows similar levels of oxidation and grain boundary degradation compared to the uncoated samples—the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractRefractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are emerging materials with potential for use under extreme conditions. As a newly developed material system, a comprehensive understanding of their long-term stability under potential service temperatures remains to be established. This study examined a titanium-vanadium-niobium-tantalum alloy, a promising RHEA known for its superior high-temperature strength and room-temperature ductility. Using a combination of advanced analytical microscopies, Calculation of Phase Diagrams (CALPHAD) software, and nanoindentation, we investigated the evolution of its microstructure and mechanical properties upon aging at 700°C. Trace interstitials such as oxygen and nitrogen, initially contributing to solid solution strengthening, promote phase segregation during thermal aging. As a result of the depletion of solute interstitials within the metal matrix, a progressive softening is observed in the alloy as a function of aging time. This study, therefore, underscores the need for a better control of impurities in future development and application of RHEAs. The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen to analyze the effect of each constituent elemental by the subtraction method and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were studied. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. According to the experiment results, the effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on mechanical properties of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys were described. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add an element which interacts frequently with the alloy, such as Mo.
